title: Honour Within the Household of God
summary: Paul directs Timothy to correct members as family, honour and support true widows, sustain and discipline elders justly, and guard his own purity and health.
historicalContext: Paul writes to Timothy at Ephesus, where a congregation meeting in homes faced pressing questions of care and order. A widow in the Greco-Roman world often had little means of earning a living, and her security depended on sons, grandsons, or a second marriage. Israel’s Scriptures had long named God the defender of the widow and built her support into the tithe and the harvest laws, and the church in Jerusalem had already organized a daily distribution for widows. At Ephesus the church’s generosity could be strained by families who shifted their duty onto the congregation and by younger widows drawn into idleness, gossip, and the false teaching that was moving from house to house. Elders who preached and taught needed support, yet leaders were also targets of rumor. Timothy, still young in the eyes of many, had to correct older members, weigh accusations, and appoint men without haste.
literaryContext: Chapter 5 opens the letter’s instructions for particular groups within “the house of God” (3:15), a section that runs through 6:2. Having urged Timothy to be an example and to give himself to reading, exhortation, and doctrine (4:12-16), Paul now shows how that ministry touches people of different ages and situations. Verses 1-2 set the family tone for all correction. Verses 3-16, the longest treatment of any group in the letter, move from family duty toward widows (3-8), to the church’s roll of older widows (9-10), to counsel for younger widows (11-15), and back to family responsibility (16). The word “honour” then links the widows to the elders (17-25), who are to be supported, protected from careless accusation, publicly corrected when guilty, and appointed only after their character has been tested. A brief personal word about Timothy’s health interrupts the counsel on appointment before Paul resumes and completes it.
themes: The church as God’s household and family
Family duty as a form of godliness
Fair support and fair discipline for elders
Impartial judgment under the eye of heaven
Purity, health, and character proved by time

outline.title: Exhorting the Family of Faith
outline.summary: Timothy is to correct older and younger members as fathers, mothers, brothers, and sisters, with complete purity toward younger women.

outline.title: Widows and the Duty of Families
outline.summary: The church honours widows who are truly alone and hoping in God, while children and grandchildren must first provide for their own.

outline.title: Enrolled Widows and Younger Widows
outline.summary: Only older widows of proven faithfulness are placed on the church’s roll; younger widows are counselled to remarry, and believing families relieve their own.

outline.title: Honour and Accountability for Elders
outline.summary: Elders who lead well, especially in preaching and teaching, deserve generous support, protection from unproven charges, and public correction when guilty.

outline.title: Impartial Judgment and Patient Discernment
outline.summary: Under a solemn charge, Timothy must judge without favouritism, appoint without haste, keep himself pure, care for his health, and let time reveal character.

verses.bibleText: Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul moves from Timothy’s personal example (4:12-16) to the way he must handle the congregation. A young leader charged to “command and teach” (4:11) could fail in two directions: shrinking from correction altogether, or delivering it with a hard edge that wounds more than it heals. Here the apostle governs the manner. “Rebuke not” renders a verb that once meant to strike at someone. It describes a harsh verbal assault, a dressing-down meant to crush, and Paul forbids it, above all toward an older man.

The “elder” of this verse is a man advanced in years rather than an officer of the church. The pairing with “younger men,” “elder women,” and “the younger” shows that Paul is sorting the congregation by age and sex; the office of elder receives its own instructions from verse 17. Age does not place anyone beyond correction, since older believers can drift as truly as the young. When Timothy must address an older brother, however, he is to “intreat him as a father.” The fifth commandment and the Levitical charge to rise before the gray head (Leviticus 19:32) stand behind the counsel. Respect governs the tone, the setting, and the words, while the truth itself is left intact.

“Intreat” comes from the same family of words Paul has just used for Timothy’s public exhortation (4:13). What the minister urges from the reading desk he now presses person to person, with the warmth that the relationship deserves.

The younger men are to be addressed “as brethren.” Timothy stands beside them, not over them. Jesus had declared that whoever does the Father’s will is his brother and sister and mother (Matthew 12:50), and the church Paul calls “the house of God” (3:15) is meant to live as that family. Correction offered in this spirit aims at restoration (Galatians 6:1). It refuses both flattery and contempt and reflects the patience of the Lord, who disciplines his children because he loves them.

wordNotes.explanation: Found only here in the New Testament, the verb carries the picture of striking a blow and was used for severe, cutting reproof. Paul is not forbidding all correction, for the next clause supplies the proper alternative. He forbids the harsh, humiliating censure that treats an older man as an offender to be beaten down rather than a father to be won.

The verb spans appeal, exhortation, and encouragement. It is the action of one who comes alongside to urge another toward what is right. Because Paul links the related noun with public teaching in 4:13 and uses the verb again in 6:2, the word implies that the content of Christian truth is being applied, not merely that feelings are being soothed. The present tense describes an ongoing pastoral habit.

verses.bibleText: The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The verb “intreat” from verse 1 still governs the sentence. Timothy is to appeal to “the elder women as mothers,” giving them the gratitude, tenderness, and honour a son owes the woman who raised him. Paul practised what he urged; he could greet the mother of Rufus as “his mother and mine” (Romans 16:13), a woman whose care had made her family to him.

“The younger as sisters” extends the family picture, and Paul adds a qualifying phrase: “with all purity.” Although the words could cover every relationship in the verse, they fit most naturally with the last group. Pastoral work brings a man into private conversations, homes, and moments of emotional need. Paul knows the human heart and does not pretend that a minister is immune to temptation. The word for purity, already required of Timothy in 4:12, includes sexual chastity, and “all” stretches it to thought, speech, touch, and the appearance of conduct. Elsewhere Paul warns that the false teachers were creeping into houses and captivating vulnerable women (2 Timothy 3:6); Timothy’s ministry must be the clear opposite.

The sibling image is itself a safeguard. A brother guards his sister’s honour and would be ashamed to exploit her trust. Wise boundaries, openness, and accountability are not signs of suspicion among believers; they protect both the minister and those he serves, and they keep the name of Christ free from reproach.

wordNotes.term: ἐν πάσῃ ἁγνείᾳ (en pasē hagneia) — with all purity
wordNotes.explanation: Hagneia denotes moral purity and, in contexts such as this, chastity in particular. The same noun appears among the marks of Timothy’s example in 4:12. Joined with “all,” it calls for purity without exception, extending beyond outward acts to motives and to conduct that could be misread. Here it shapes a minister’s relationships with younger women.

verses.bibleText: Honour widows that are widows indeed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now begins the longest instruction about any group in the letter. The attention given to widows reflects the reality of the ancient world. A woman whose husband died often lost her main source of income and protection; respectable paid work was scarce, and property frequently passed through male relatives. Israel’s God had made himself known as “a judge of the widows” (Psalm 68:5) and had written their support into the tithe of the third year and the gleaning laws (Deuteronomy 14:28-29; 24:19-21). The first organizational crisis of the church concerned the daily distribution to widows (Acts 6:1).

The command is brief: “Honour widows.” The verb includes respect, but it plainly reaches to material provision. Jesus used the honour owed to parents in the fifth commandment to include financial support, and he condemned those who evaded it by religious technicalities (Matthew 15:4-6). The same root returns in verse 17, where the “double honour” given to elders is tied to wages. By calling relief “honour,” Paul removes the stigma that so often clings to dependence. The widow who receives the church’s help is treated as one deserving dignity, not as an object of pity.

The qualifying phrase “that are widows indeed” introduces discernment. Paul does not deny that other bereaved women are widows; he identifies those for whom the congregation must take responsibility. The verses that follow define them: women without children or grandchildren to support them (verse 4), who are left alone and have set their hope on God (verse 5), and who are not living for self-indulgence (verse 6). Love that is wise asks where the need is real and who is best placed to meet it, so that the church’s resources reach those with no other help.

wordNotes.explanation: The present imperative of timaō, the verb used in the Greek Old Testament for honouring father and mother. In this passage it carries both esteem and tangible support, as the references to family provision (verses 4, 8, 16) and to wages for elders (verses 17-18) confirm. The honour is meant to be continual and practical.

The adverb ontōs means “really” or “truly.” Paul uses it to mark widows who are such in the full sense, without family resources and wholly dependent on God and his people. The phrase recurs in verses 5 and 16 and frames the entire discussion of who should receive the congregation’s regular care.

verses.bibleText: But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The first category is the widow who has living descendants. The King James word “nephews” reflects older English usage, in which the term could mean grandchildren or descendants generally; the Greek refers to offspring beyond the first generation. Paul’s plural verb, “let them learn,” shows that the children and grandchildren are the ones being instructed. The widow herself is described, but the family is addressed.

What they must learn is “to shew piety at home.” The verb is the action form of eusebeia, “godliness,” the great word of this letter (2:2; 3:16; 4:7-8; 6:6). Paul thus places care for an aging mother inside the life of godliness, not beside it. True religion begins with the people under one’s own roof. The word “first” sets the priority. No amount of public religious activity can substitute for neglected parents, a point Jesus pressed against those who dedicated money to God while leaving father and mother in want (Mark 7:10-13).

They are also to “requite their parents,” to make a return for what they received. The term for parents can embrace grandparents and earlier generations. Years of feeding, nursing, teaching, and sacrifice create a debt no child can fully repay, and Paul treats repayment as a continuing obligation. Yet the motive he supplies is higher than obligation: “that is good and acceptable before God.” The phrase echoes 2:3, where prayer for all people is “acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour.” The same God who welcomes the church’s intercession welcomes the son who changes his schedule to care for his mother.

Modern provisions for the elderly do not cancel the principle. Circumstances differ, and families may need to share care with others, but believers are called to see the needs of aging parents and grandparents as a sacred trust, and to meet them with gratitude rather than resentment.

wordNotes.explanation: This verb, used elsewhere in the New Testament only in Acts 17:23 of worship, is related to eusebeia, the letter’s key term for godliness. Here it describes reverent duty expressed in family care. The construction with “their own house” shows that devotion to God is to be lived out first toward one’s own household.

Literally “to give back returns.” Amoibē, a word found only here in the New Testament, means recompense; the verb means to render what is due. The present infinitive points to an ongoing practice of repayment to parents and grandparents for the care received in childhood.

verses.bibleText: Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now defines the widow for whom the church is responsible. She is “desolate,” a perfect participle meaning that she has been left alone and remains so. In contrast with the widow of verse 4, no children or grandchildren stand ready to support her. Her bereavement has stripped away both husband and family, and she lives exposed to want.

Yet Paul describes her chiefly by her faith: she “trusteth in God.” The perfect tense pictures hope that was fixed on God at some past point and continues to rest there. She has not turned to schemes for survival or to the attentions of others; she has placed her future in the hands of the One who “relieveth the fatherless and widow” (Psalm 146:9). The congregation that cares for her becomes the means by which her hope in God is honoured.

Her trust expresses itself in “supplications and prayers night and day.” These are the same two words Paul used when calling the whole church to pray for all people (2:1). The widow indeed embodies what every believer is summoned to do. Anna, a widow of great age who “served God with fastings and prayers night and day” in the temple (Luke 2:37), offers an earlier picture of the same devotion. “Night and day” describes constancy, a life in which prayer is the habitual atmosphere, rather than an unbroken round of hours on her knees.

The arrangement Paul envisions is mutual. The church supplies the widow’s bread, and the widow, freed from the anxious search for support, carries the church in prayer. Her loneliness becomes the setting for ministry. Those who seem to have nothing to give may in fact be among the congregation’s strongest intercessors.

wordNotes.explanation: A perfect passive participle of monoō, “to make alone,” occurring only here in the New Testament. It describes a woman who has been left on her own and continues in that condition, without husband or the family support described in verse 4.

wordNotes.term: ἤλπικεν ἐπὶ θεόν (ēlpiken epi theon) — trusteth in God
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “has set her hope on God.” The perfect tense describes hope that was placed and still remains. Biblical hope combines confident expectation with patient waiting. Paul uses the same construction in 4:10 of his own ministry and in 6:17 of the hope the rich must place in the living God rather than in uncertain wealth.

verses.bibleText: But she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A second kind of widow stands in sharp contrast. She “liveth in pleasure,” a phrase describing a life given over to luxury and self-gratification. James uses the same verb of the rich who have lived in pleasure on the earth (James 5:5), and the Greek Old Testament applies it to Sodom’s pride and ease (Ezekiel 16:49). Paul does not specify her conduct. It might involve relationships that traded intimacy for support, or a round of amusement and indulgence. In either case the self has replaced God at the centre.

Paul’s verdict is a paradox: she “is dead while she liveth.” Her body is alive, and she may appear to be enjoying life to the full, but before God she is already dead. The perfect tense describes a settled condition. The church at Sardis had a name that it lived and was dead (Revelation 3:1), and the father of the prodigal said of his son, “this my son was dead” (Luke 15:24).

The practical consequence is that such a woman is not a “widow indeed” and should not be placed on the church’s roll. But the verse also holds out an implicit appeal. Those who were dead in trespasses and sins have been made alive in Christ (Ephesians 2:1-5). The same voice that pronounces the verdict can still raise the dead.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb spatalaō means to live luxuriously or self-indulgently. It describes a manner of life devoted to comfort and gratification. Its only other New Testament use describes the wealthy who fattened their hearts while defrauding labourers.

verses.bibleText: And these things give in charge, that they may be blameless.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These things” gathers up the instruction of verses 3-6, especially the duty of children and grandchildren toward their widowed mothers and grandmothers. Paul uses the verb “give in charge,” the same word for authoritative command found in 1:3 and 4:11. Family care is not left to private preference; Timothy is to announce it to the congregation as an apostolic requirement.

The purpose is “that they may be blameless.” The plural most naturally refers to the descendants addressed in verse 4, though the widows described in verses 5-6 are not far from view. The adjective is the same one required of the overseer in 3:2. What Paul demands of leaders he now expects of ordinary households: a life that gives no one a just ground for accusation. A church in which grown children neglect their parents invites the scorn of neighbours who honour their own. The gospel is commended or discredited by the way believers treat the old and the vulnerable within their own families (Titus 2:5; 1 Peter 2:12).

wordNotes.explanation: The word describes someone against whom no charge can fairly be brought, literally one who cannot be laid hold of. It occurs in the New Testament only in 1 Timothy: of the overseer (3:2), of the families here, and of Timothy’s keeping of the commandment until Christ’s appearing (6:14).

verses.bibleText: But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here Paul states the gravest consequence of family neglect. The verb “provide” means to think ahead and plan for someone’s needs; Paul uses it elsewhere of providing things honest in the sight of all (Romans 12:17; 2 Corinthians 8:21). The circle of obligation has two rings. “His own” embraces relatives more broadly, while “those of his own house” singles out the immediate household, with “specially” marking the stronger claim of the nearer bond.

The person who fails here “hath denied the faith.” Paul is not describing a spoken renunciation of Christianity. Conduct can deny what the lips confess, and Titus 1:16 speaks of those who “profess that they know God; but in works they deny him.” The faith here is the body of Christian truth, which includes the command to honour father and mother and the whole ethic of self-giving love. To neglect one’s dependants while professing that faith is to contradict it in practice. Faith that does not work by love (Galatians 5:6) is a counterfeit.

Such a person is also “worse than an infidel.” Many in the pagan world regarded the support of aged parents as a sacred duty; Roman and Greek moralists alike treated filial neglect as shameful. Paul recognizes that God’s law is written in some measure on the hearts even of those without the Scriptures (Romans 2:14-15). A believer who has the fifth commandment, the teaching of Jesus, and the example of Christ himself, who in his dying hour committed his mother to the beloved disciple (John 19:26-27), has far less excuse.

The verse condemns unwillingness, not poverty. Some believers cannot do all they wish for their families, and the church exists in part to help them. But no one who claims Christ may treat the needs of parents, spouse, or children as someone else’s problem. Love begins with the household of faith and, within it, with one’s own household (Galatians 6:10).

wordNotes.explanation: The verb pronoeō combines “before” and “think,” describing forethought that plans and supplies what others will need. It implies active, responsible care, not a grudging response to emergencies. Paul uses it in Romans 12:17 and 2 Corinthians 8:21 for taking thought to act honourably before others.

The perfect tense of arneomai, to deny or disown. In the Pastorals the verb repeatedly describes a denial carried out in life and conduct rather than by words alone (2 Timothy 3:5; Titus 1:16; 2:12). Neglecting one’s family is treated as a practical repudiation of the faith one professes.

verses.bibleText: Let not a widow be taken into the number under threescore years old, having been the wife of one man,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul turns from the family’s duty to the congregation’s own arrangements. “Let not a widow be taken into the number” assumes a formal list. The verb means to enrol or register, and it was used of entering names on a roster, such as soldiers enlisted for service. Whether this roll constituted a recognized order of widows is uncertain. The qualifications that follow, and the pledge implied in verse 12, suggest that enrolled widows received regular support and were expected to devote themselves to prayer and practical service, but the passage does not describe an office in the way chapter 3 describes overseers and deacons.

The first qualification is age: not “under threescore years old.” Sixty was commonly regarded in the ancient world as the threshold of old age. By that point remarriage was unlikely and the ability to earn a living had largely passed. Paul does not imply that a destitute widow of forty was left without help; verse 16 and the command of verse 3 cover her. He is defining who may be placed on the permanent roll, where the church undertook long-term responsibility and the widow, in turn, committed herself to the Lord’s service.

The second qualification is that she has been “the wife of one man.” The phrase mirrors the requirement for overseers and deacons in 3:2 and 3:12. Because Paul will shortly urge younger widows to remarry (verse 14), it is unlikely that he means to exclude a woman who, following that very counsel, married again and was widowed a second time. The phrase most naturally describes a faithful, devoted wife whose married life was marked by fidelity.

The list honours faithfulness. A congregation that sets such a standard declares that a life of quiet loyalty in marriage and home is worthy of public recognition, and that those who have given themselves to others will not be forgotten when they themselves are in need.

wordNotes.term: καταλεγέσθω (katalegesthō) — be taken into the number
wordNotes.explanation: A present passive imperative of katalegō, found only here in the New Testament. In wider Greek it was used for selecting and enrolling people on a list, including soldiers. Its use here implies a recognized register of widows whom the church committed itself to support.

wordNotes.term: ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνή (henos andros gynē) — the wife of one man
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase is the counterpart of “the husband of one wife” required of overseers and deacons. Its focus is the character of the marriage, a woman known for faithfulness to her husband. In the light of Paul’s counsel that younger widows remarry, it is best read as a demand for marital fidelity rather than a ban on a second marriage after bereavement.

verses.bibleText: Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third qualification is a proven reputation: she must be “well reported of for good works.” The verb means to be attested by witnesses. Like the deacons of Acts 6:3 and the overseer who must have “a good report of them which are without” (3:7), the enrolled widow must be known by her record. Good works run through the letter as the expected fruit of saving faith (2:10; 6:18). They do not purchase God’s grace; they show that it has been received.

Paul then lists examples. She has “brought up children,” whether her own or orphans taken into her care. She has “lodged strangers,” opening her home to travelling believers and messengers of the gospel, a vital service when inns were often unsafe and immoral (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2). She has “washed the saints’ feet,” performing the lowliest task of hospitality for weary guests. The phrase recalls the Lord who rose from supper, girded himself with a towel, and told his disciples to follow his example (John 13:14-15). The church’s own practice of foot washing in the ordinance of humility carries forward that same lesson. She has “relieved the afflicted,” coming to the aid of those under pressure of poverty, illness, or persecution. And she has “diligently followed every good work,” pursuing well-doing as a settled direction of life.

The list is strikingly ordinary. Child-rearing, hospitality, humble service, and help for the distressed are the daily labours of a godly home, mostly unseen by the wider world. Paul treats them as worthy of the church’s honour. There is also a beautiful reciprocity. The woman who once opened her door to strangers and fed the needy now has her own needs met by the family she served. Her past ministry also suits her for continued usefulness, since she already knows how to care for children, guests, and the afflicted.

wordNotes.term: εἰ ἁγίων πόδας ἔνιψεν (ei hagiōn podas enipsen) — if she have washed the saints’ feet
wordNotes.explanation: Washing a guest’s feet was a menial courtesy usually performed by a servant (Luke 7:44). A hostess who did it herself showed humility and love. Directed to “the saints,” fellow believers, the act also echoes Jesus’ example in the upper room, where he washed his disciples’ feet and commanded them to do as he had done.

The verb eparkeō means to help or give aid sufficient for a need. Its only other New Testament uses come in verse 16, where believing families are told to relieve their own widows so that the church can relieve the truly destitute. The enrolled widow has done for others what the church now does for her.

verses.bibleText: But the younger widows refuse: for when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But the younger widows refuse” means that Timothy is to decline enrolling them on the list. The verb is the same one used in 4:7 for refusing profane and old wives’ fables. Paul is not withholding compassion from a young widow in distress. Verses 3 and 16 make clear that the needy are to be helped. He is excluding younger women from the permanent roll and the pledge that accompanied it.

His first reason is stated in vivid terms: “when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry.” The verb, found nowhere else in the Bible, combines a word for strong physical desire with a prefix meaning “against.” Some hear in it the picture of a young animal pulling restlessly against the yoke. A younger widow who had committed herself to serve Christ as an enrolled widow might later find natural desire for a husband pulling her away from that commitment. The desire itself is not condemned. Marriage is God’s gift, and Paul will urge these very women to marry (verse 14). The difficulty lies in the collision between a pledge made in the first grief of bereavement and the ordinary longings of a young woman’s life.

Paul’s counsel shows pastoral realism. He refuses to lay on people a vow they are unlikely to keep, and he has already warned that false teachers were forbidding marriage (4:3). Later centuries often exalted perpetual widowhood and celibacy as a higher spiritual state; Paul here resists that tendency. Elsewhere he acknowledges that “it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9) and that he does not wish to cast a snare upon anyone (1 Corinthians 7:35). The wise shepherd fits the commitment to the person and her season of life.

wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of paraiteomai, to decline or reject a request. In the Pastorals it is used of refusing myths (4:7), foolish questions (2 Timothy 2:23), and a divisive person after warning (Titus 3:10). Here it directs Timothy to decline enrolling younger widows, not to deny them aid.

wordNotes.term: καταστρηνιάσωσιν τοῦ Χριστοῦ (katastrēniasōsin tou Christou) — wax wanton against Christ
wordNotes.explanation: The simple verb strēniaō describes living in sensual vigour or indulgence (Revelation 18:7, 9). Prefixed with kata and followed by the genitive, it pictures desire that moves against Christ, here pulling an enrolled widow away from the commitment she had made to his service.

verses.bibleText: Having damnation, because they have cast off their first faith.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Having damnation” uses an English word that in 1611 could mean judgment or condemnation in a general sense. The Greek term is krima, a verdict or judgment, the same word used in 3:6 for the “condemnation of the devil” into which a proud novice might fall. In this context it describes the censure that rightly falls on one who breaks a solemn commitment; it does not declare that remarriage consigns a widow to eternal ruin. Paul’s own counsel to marry in verse 14 rules that out.

The reason for the judgment is that “they have cast off their first faith.” The word for faith can mean a pledge or solemn promise, and that sense fits the passage. On enrolment, a widow apparently committed herself to remain unmarried and to devote herself to Christ’s service. To set that pledge aside for a new marriage was to treat a promise made to the Lord as disposable. The verb means to nullify or set aside, as one might annul an agreement (Galatians 3:15). Some understand “first faith” as the widow’s original faith in Christ, abandoned through marriage to an unbeliever, but the contrast with verse 14 points to a specific pledge.

Scripture treats vows to God with great seriousness: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). That is precisely why Paul is so careful about who takes this one. Leaders should not rush people into commitments beyond their maturity, and believers are to keep their word as God keeps his.

wordNotes.explanation: Krima denotes a judgment or verdict, often an adverse one. Its weight depends on context. Here it refers to the censure incurred by breaking a pledge to Christ, not to a sentence of final destruction. Modern versions commonly render it “condemnation” or “judgment.”

wordNotes.term: τὴν πρώτην πίστιν ἠθέτησαν (tēn prōtēn pistin ēthetēsan) — cast off their first faith
wordNotes.explanation: Pistis can mean trust, the body of belief, or a pledge of fidelity. With the verb atheteō, “set aside” or “annul,” it most likely describes the earlier commitment made on enrolment as a widow devoted to Christ’s service, a promise now broken by choosing remarriage.

verses.bibleText: And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s second reason for declining younger widows concerns what regular support without settled responsibility can produce. “They learn to be idle”: the verb describes a habit acquired through practice. A young woman supported by the church and without a clear sphere of work could gradually learn idleness the way others learn a trade.

They go “wandering about from house to house.” Enrolled widows may have visited homes as part of their service, and those visits could easily become occasions for carrying news from one door to the next. They become “tattlers,” people who talk nonsense and spread idle chatter; John uses the related verb of Diotrephes “prating against us with malicious words” (3 John 1:10). They become “busybodies,” meddling in matters that are not theirs. The same word describes the “curious arts” of the Ephesian magicians who burned their books (Acts 19:19), and Paul plays on its root when he rebukes those at Thessalonica who were “working not at all, but are busybodies” (2 Thessalonians 3:11).

They end by “speaking things which they ought not.” The phrase is close to Titus 1:11, where false teachers subvert households by “teaching things which they ought not.” Paul may well fear that idle visitors were becoming carriers of the very speculations troubling Ephesus (4:1-7; 2 Timothy 3:6-7).

The warning is not a verdict on women as such. Paul rebukes the same faults in men. The principle is broader: unoccupied time and unguarded speech are dangerous companions, and meaningful work is one of God’s gifts for keeping both heart and tongue in order (Proverbs 31:27).

wordNotes.explanation: Argos, from a- and ergon, means “without work,” inactive or unproductive. Paul says these women “learn” to be idle, describing a settled habit formed over time. The same adjective appears in Titus 1:12 in the proverb about the Cretans and in Jesus’ warning about every idle word (Matthew 12:36).

wordNotes.term: φλύαροι καὶ περίεργοι (phluaroi kai periergoi) — tattlers and busybodies
wordNotes.explanation: Phluaros describes one who talks foolishly or spreads idle gossip. Periergos describes one who is overly busy about others’ concerns, a meddler; in Acts 19:19 the same word refers to magical arts. Together they portray restless talk that intrudes where it does not belong.

verses.bibleText: I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“I will therefore” introduces Paul’s positive counsel, drawn as a conclusion from the dangers just described. The verb expresses an apostolic wish carrying real authority, as in 2:8. The context identifies “the younger women” as the younger widows of verses 11-13. Paul is advising a particular group in a particular situation, not issuing a rule that every young woman must marry.

His counsel has three parts. They are to “marry,” entering again the relationship God instituted at creation (Genesis 2:18, 24). They are to “bear children,” embracing the blessing of family life. And they are to “guide the house,” a strong term that means to manage or rule a household. The word gives the wife and mother real authority within her sphere, the kind of capable oversight displayed by the woman of Proverbs 31, who buys fields, trades, cares for the poor, and “looketh well to the ways of her household” (Proverbs 31:27).

Some have sensed tension with 1 Corinthians 7, where Paul commends the unmarried state. There is no real contradiction. In Corinth Paul expressed a personal preference for singleness among those so gifted, while plainly permitting a widow to remarry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). Here he applies the same principle: each must live according to the gift God has given, and for most younger widows that gift is marriage. His counsel also stands against the false teachers who forbade marriage (4:3). Scripture holds marriage “honourable in all” (Hebrews 13:4).

The aim is to “give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully.” The word for occasion was used for a military base of operations, a foothold from which an attack is launched. The adversary may be a human opponent watching for scandal, or Satan himself, whom the next verse names. In either case Paul wants the conduct of believing women, like that of overseers (3:7) and wives in Titus 2:5, to deny the critics any ground for slander. A well-ordered Christian home becomes a public testimony to the gospel.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb combines “house” and “master” and means to manage or rule a household. It is related to the noun oikodespotēs, “householder,” used in Jesus’ parables (Matthew 13:52; 20:1). Here it assigns to the wife and mother a position of genuine responsibility and authority in directing the home.

Aphormē originally described a starting point or base of operations for a military campaign, and came to mean an opportunity or pretext. Paul uses it of sin seizing an occasion through the commandment (Romans 7:8) and of liberty becoming an occasion for the flesh (Galatians 5:13).

verses.bibleText: For some are already turned aside after Satan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s counsel is not theoretical. “For some are already turned aside after Satan.” The word “already” gives urgency to everything he has said; the dangers of verses 11-13 had become realities in the congregation.

“Turned aside” is the letter’s recurring term for defection. Some had “turned aside unto vain jangling” (1:6), and later Paul warns that people will “be turned unto fables” (2 Timothy 4:4). These younger widows had not merely made poor choices; they had begun following “after Satan,” going behind him as a disciple follows a teacher. Whether their departure involved immorality, the speculative teaching that Paul traces to “seducing spirits” (4:1), or both, the source was the same adversary who opposes Christ and his people.

The verse sets church life within the great controversy between Christ and Satan. Idleness, gossip, and broken pledges become openings for the enemy. Yet even here hope remains. Paul had delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan so that they might “learn not to blaspheme” (1:20),. The One who came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8) can bring back those who have turned aside.

wordNotes.explanation: From ektrepō, “to turn out of the way.” In the Pastorals the verb repeatedly describes departure from sound teaching and godly life into error (1:6; 6:20; 2 Timothy 4:4). Followed here by “after Satan,” it marks a turning from Christ to follow his adversary.

verses.bibleText: If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul closes the section on widows by returning to family responsibility. Many ancient manuscripts read simply “if any woman that believeth have widows,” while the text behind the King James Version includes “man or.” The shorter reading probably singles out believing women because the daily care of a widowed mother, mother-in-law, or other relative usually fell to the women of a household. It may also have in view a woman of means, perhaps herself widowed, who could support others as Dorcas did (Acts 9:36-39). Either way, verse 8 has already laid the same duty on men.

Such a believer is to “relieve them,” supplying what they need. The goal is stated twice. Negatively: “let not the church be charged,” that is, weighed down with a burden that belongs to the family. Positively: “that it may relieve them that are widows indeed.” The congregation’s resources were limited, and every widow supported by her own family freed the church to care for one who had no one at all.

The verse rounds off the section where it began, with honour for widows indeed (verse 3). It also shows that family care and church care are partners. When relatives do their part, the church can concentrate on the friendless; when the church does its part, no widow is forgotten. Wise stewardship of a congregation’s help is itself an act of love, ensuring that generosity reaches the people it was meant to bless (Galatians 6:10).

wordNotes.explanation: The feminine adjective “believing,” used as a noun for a Christian woman. Luke uses the same word of Timothy’s mother, “a certain woman, which was a Jewess, and believed” (Acts 16:1), and of Lydia, whom Paul judged “faithful to the Lord” (Acts 16:15). The better-attested reading here addresses believing women specifically.

wordNotes.term: μὴ βαρείσθω (mē bareisthō) — let not … be charged
wordNotes.explanation: The verb bareō means to weigh down or burden. Paul uses related forms when he says he laboured night and day so as not to be “chargeable” to the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8). Here it describes the financial and practical load the church should be spared when families can carry it.

verses.bibleText: Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now turns from widows to elders, linking the two sections with the word “honour.” Here “elders” denotes church officers, the same leaders called overseers in 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-7 uses both titles for one office. They are those who “rule,” a verb meaning to stand before, to lead and also to care for. Paul used it of a man who manages his own house well (3:4-5) and of those who are “over you in the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 5:12). The word “well” sets the measure. Office alone does not earn this honour; faithful leadership does.

Such elders are “counted worthy of double honour.” As in verse 3, honour includes both respect and material support, and verse 18 settles the matter by speaking of wages. “Double” may mean ample or generous honour, or a twofold honour of esteem and remuneration together. Paul is not setting a precise salary scale. He is insisting that faithful leaders receive a generous measure of both regard and support.

The honour is due “especially” to those “who labour in the word and doctrine.” The verb for labour means to toil to the point of weariness; Paul uses it of his own exhausting ministry (4:10; Colossians 1:29). Preaching the word and teaching sound doctrine demand study, prayer, and pastoral effort that leave little time for earning a living by other means. While every overseer must be “apt to teach” (3:2), some gave themselves especially to this work.

Behind the counsel stands God’s provision for the Levites, who received the tithe of Israel in return for their service at the sanctuary (Numbers 18:21). Paul draws the same line in 1 Corinthians 9:13-14: “even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.” Faithful support of the ministry is part of the church’s obedience. At the same time, the honour is tied to ruling well and labouring hard, and the letter has already warned that the overseer must not be greedy of gain (3:3). Generous congregations and selfless ministers belong together.

wordNotes.explanation: Timē means honour or esteem, and also price or payment. Here, as verse 18 shows, it includes compensation. Diplous, “double,” may express generous measure or the twofold nature of the honour, respect joined with material support. Either way the elder who leads well is to be valued and provided for.

Kopiaō means to work hard, to toil until weary. Paul often applies it to his own ministry and to the work of other leaders (1 Corinthians 15:10; Colossians 1:29; 1 Thessalonians 5:12). Used with “in the word and doctrine,” it portrays preaching and teaching as demanding, exhausting labour.

verses.bibleText: For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul grounds his counsel in an authority higher than his own: “For the scripture saith.” The first quotation comes from Deuteronomy 25:4: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn.” On the threshing floor an ox walked over the sheaves to loosen the grain, and the law forbade a muzzle that would keep it from eating as it worked. In 1 Corinthians 9:9-10 Paul draws out the principle more fully. The humane provision for animals reveals God’s concern for every labourer, and it applies with greater force to those who sow spiritual things and may rightly reap material support.

The second quotation, “The labourer is worthy of his reward,” matches word for word the saying of Jesus in Luke 10:7, spoken as he sent out the seventy (compare Matthew 10:10). Remarkably, Paul places it under the same heading as the law of Moses: “the scripture saith.” Whether he was citing Luke’s written Gospel or a collection of the Lord’s words already treasured by the church, he treats the teaching of Jesus as carrying the full authority of Scripture. Peter later speaks of Paul’s own letters in the same breath as “the other scriptures” (2 Peter 3:15-16).

The word “reward” means wages, pay rightly earned. Support for faithful ministers is therefore a matter of justice, not charity. Congregations that leave their pastors in want disobey both Moses and Christ. Yet the same Scriptures guard against the opposite danger. Elders are to feed the flock “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1 Peter 5:2). The labourer is worthy of his wages, and the faithful labourer does not work for wages first.

wordNotes.term: λέγει ἡ γραφή (legei hē graphē) — the scripture saith
wordNotes.explanation: Graphē, “writing,” refers in the New Testament to the sacred Scriptures. Paul uses this formula in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 4:30 when appealing to the Old Testament. The present tense presents Scripture as God’s word speaking now. Here the formula introduces both a Mosaic command and a saying of Jesus.

Misthos means wages or pay for work done. Jesus used it in the parable of the labourers (Matthew 20:8), and James uses it of wages unjustly withheld from harvesters (James 5:4). In this verse it frames ministerial support as a just payment owed to those who labour.

verses.bibleText: Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Leaders who preach, decide, and correct inevitably disappoint some people, and a single aggrieved voice can do great damage to a ministry. Paul therefore instructs Timothy: “Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.” The verb “receive” means to admit or entertain. Timothy is not to open formal proceedings, or even give a charge serious credence, on the word of one person alone.

The requirement of two or three witnesses comes from the law of Moses: “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15; compare 17:6). Jesus built the same safeguard into his instructions for church discipline (Matthew 18:16), and Paul invoked it before his third visit to Corinth (2 Corinthians 13:1). The principle protected every Israelite. Paul does not invent a privilege for leaders; he insists that the protection owed to all be applied with particular care to those whose position makes them frequent targets of rumour, resentment, and misrepresentation.

The verse does not shelter wrongdoing, as verse 20 immediately shows. It shelters the truth. Moses faced the murmuring of Korah’s company (Numbers 16:1-3), and the law warned, “Thou shalt not raise a false report” (Exodus 23:1). Congregations today honour this verse when they refuse to pass along unverified stories about their pastors, when they direct complaints through proper channels, and when they insist on evidence before judgment. Such care guards the reputation of the innocent and the integrity of the whole body.

wordNotes.explanation: Katēgoria is a formal charge, the term used in legal settings for bringing someone to account. Pilate asked, “What accusation bring ye against this man?” (John 18:29). The word implies more than a complaint; it is an accusation that would require a response.

wordNotes.term: ἐπὶ δύο ἢ τριῶν μαρτύρων (epi duo ē triōn marturōn) — before two or three witnesses
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition epi here means “on the basis of” the testimony of witnesses. The wording reflects Deuteronomy 19:15 and is echoed in Matthew 18:16, 2 Corinthians 13:1, and Hebrews 10:28. At least two independent witnesses must support a charge before it can be accepted.

verses.bibleText: Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Protection from false accusation does not mean immunity from true ones. “Them that sin rebuke before all.” The context still concerns elders, though the principle applies more widely. The present participle describes those whose sin has been established and who stand guilty, and it may suggest persistence in wrongdoing after private appeals have failed (Matthew 18:15-17).

The verb “rebuke” means to expose and convict, bringing sin to light with evidence so that the offender is called to repentance. It differs from the harsh censure forbidden in verse 1. The Spirit convicts the world of sin (John 16:8); believers are to reprove the works of darkness (Ephesians 5:11); Timothy is to “reprove, rebuke, exhort” (2 Timothy 4:2).

“Before all” may mean before the other elders or before the whole congregation. The pattern of Matthew 18:17, “tell it unto the church,” favours the latter, especially when a leader’s sin has public consequences. Paul himself confronted Peter “before them all” when his conduct misled others (Galatians 2:14). The purpose is “that others also may fear.” Deuteronomy uses similar language when it says that all Israel shall hear and fear (Deuteronomy 13:11; 19:20), and after the judgment on Ananias and Sapphira great fear came upon the church (Acts 5:11).

Leaders who teach others receive the stricter judgment (James 3:1). A church that hides the sins of its leaders betrays both the victims of those sins and the leaders themselves, for concealment leaves them unrepentant. Public correction, carried out with grief and with restoration as its aim, keeps the church honest before God and the world.

wordNotes.explanation: Elenchō means to bring to light, to convict, or to reprove by showing someone their fault. It assumes that the evidence is clear and aims at repentance. The same verb describes the Spirit’s work of convicting the world (John 16:8) and the duty to expose the works of darkness (Ephesians 5:11).

Literally “may have fear.” The phrase describes a healthy dread of sin and its consequences awakened by seeing discipline carried out. It echoes the Deuteronomic purpose of public judgment, that all who hear should fear and refrain from evil.

verses.bibleText: I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The tone suddenly becomes solemn. “I charge thee” uses a verb for earnest testimony given under oath, the language of a courtroom. Paul invokes three witnesses: God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels. Timothy is to understand that his handling of accusations and discipline takes place in the presence of the Judge of all the earth and of the Son, to whom the Father has committed all judgment (John 5:22).

The “elect angels” are the holy angels who remained loyal to God when others fell (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 1:6). Scripture presents them as interested observers of the church’s life (1 Corinthians 4:9; 1 Peter 1:12) and as participants in the scenes of judgment and of Christ’s return (Daniel 7:10; Matthew 25:31). The phrase sets Timothy’s decisions within the great controversy between good and evil.

The charge is that Timothy observe “these things,” the instructions about accusation and rebuke in verses 19-20, “without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality.” The first phrase forbids prejudgment, deciding a case before the evidence is heard. The second forbids leaning toward someone because of friendship, wealth, status, or influence. A young leader would face both pressures: the temptation to protect respected friends and the temptation to side with the powerful in order to be accepted. James condemns the congregation that seats the rich man in honour and the poor man on the floor (James 2:1-4). Moses told Israel’s judges, “Ye shall not respect persons in judgment… for the judgment is God’s” (Deuteronomy 1:17). Because the Lord shows no partiality (Acts 10:34), those who act in his name must not show it either.

wordNotes.explanation: The adjective “elect” or “chosen” distinguishes the faithful angels from those who sinned and were cast down. These are God’s chosen servants who carry out his will and accompany the Son of man in judgment. Invoking them heightens the solemnity of Paul’s charge.

wordNotes.term: χωρὶς προκρίματος (chōris prokrimatos) — without preferring one before another
wordNotes.explanation: Prokrima, found only here in the Bible, means a prejudgment, a verdict reached before the facts are heard. Paired with prosklisis, “partiality” or “inclination toward,” it describes the two great distortions of justice: deciding in advance and favouring one side.

verses.bibleText: Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins: keep thyself pure.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The best way to avoid painful discipline is to take care in appointment. “Lay hands suddenly on no man.” In the Pastorals the laying on of hands marks the setting apart of a person for ministry, as with Timothy himself (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6), following the pattern of Acts 6:6 and 13:3. Some understand the verse as referring to the restoration of a disciplined elder after repentance, which would also fit the preceding verses. The broader usage of the letter, however, points to ordination. Either way, the warning is against haste.

“Suddenly” means quickly, before a person’s life has been observed long enough. Paul has already said that deacons must “first be proved” (3:10) and that an overseer must not be a recent convert (3:6). Gifts, eloquence, and enthusiasm can appear quickly; character takes time to reveal itself.

“Neither be partaker of other men’s sins.” The laying on of hands was a public endorsement. Those who set an unfit man in office share responsibility for the harm he causes, much as the watchman in Ezekiel who failed to warn bore guilt for the blood of those who perished (Ezekiel 3:18). John warns that whoever welcomes a false teacher “is partaker of his evil deeds” (2 John 1:11). Timothy and the elders who joined him in ordaining could not escape accountability by pleading that they had meant well.

The verse ends with a personal command: “keep thyself pure.” The adjective is related to the noun “purity” in verse 2. One who judges others must guard his own life, lest he try to remove the speck from another’s eye while a beam remains in his own (Matthew 7:5). Churches today honour this verse when they give time to knowing candidates, weigh proven faithfulness above charisma, and pray for leaders who are themselves walking in integrity.

wordNotes.term: χεῖρας ταχέως μηδενὶ ἐπιτίθει (cheiras tacheōs mēdeni epitithei) — lay hands suddenly on no man
wordNotes.explanation: The adverb tacheōs, “quickly,” is used here in the negative sense of “hastily” or “too soon.” Laying on of hands in the Pastorals signifies public appointment to service. The present imperative with a negative forbids making such appointments a hurried practice.

wordNotes.term: σεαυτὸν ἁγνὸν τήρει (seauton hagnon tērei) — keep thyself pure
wordNotes.explanation: Hagnos means pure or chaste, free from moral defilement. The verb tēreō means to guard or keep watch over. Timothy must continually guard his own moral purity, the same quality he must look for in others. John uses hagnos of the believer who purifies himself in hope of Christ’s appearing (1 John 3:3).

verses.bibleText: Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This personal word interrupts the counsel on appointment, which resumes in verse 24. Its placement may not be accidental. Having just told Timothy to “keep thyself pure,” Paul may have feared that his conscientious colleague would take purity to require a rigid self-denial that refused even a remedy for illness. The verse reveals that Timothy had been a water-drinker. The verb Paul uses means to drink water only. Timothy’s habit placed him in a long line of consecrated servants who abstained from wine: the priests in their ministry (Leviticus 10:9), the Nazirites (Numbers 6:3), the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35:6), Daniel and his companions (Daniel 1:12), and John the Baptist (Luke 1:15). Paul does not rebuke that abstinence; he assumes it.

The exception is medical and specific. Timothy is to use wine “for thy stomach’s sake and thine often infirmities.” He suffered repeated illness, apparently including digestive trouble. In many ancient towns the water supply was contaminated, and dysentery and stomach complaints were common. Wine was widely used in the ancient world as a remedy; the Good Samaritan poured oil and wine into the traveller’s wounds (Luke 10:34). “Drink no longer water” means that Timothy should stop drinking water exclusively, not that he should stop drinking water.

The quantity is carefully limited: “a little.” Paul has already required deacons not to be “given to much wine” (3:8) and has warned elsewhere against drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18). The Greek word for wine covered the juice of the grape in various states, and in common practice wine was often heavily diluted with water. Some understand Paul to mean unfermented grape juice, consistent with Scripture’s warnings about intoxicating drink (Proverbs 20:1; 23:29-32). The text does not settle the question, but in every reading the counsel remains a small, remedial measure prescribed for a sick man.

The verse therefore offers no warrant for social or recreational drinking. It assumes that Timothy normally abstained and needed apostolic counsel even to take wine as medicine. What it does reveal is Paul’s concern for his colleague’s body. The body is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20), and physical health affects the clarity and endurance needed for ministry (3 John 1:2). Where safe water and better remedies are available today, the same principle leads believers to choose the healthiest means within reach and to practise temperance in all things.

wordNotes.term: μηκέτι ὑδροπότει (mēketi hydropotei) — drink no longer water
wordNotes.explanation: Hydropoteō, found only here in the New Testament, means to drink water only, to be a water-drinker. With mēketi, “no longer,” Paul asks Timothy to stop limiting himself to water alone, not to give up water. The Greek Old Testament uses a related expression of Daniel’s request for water instead of the king’s wine.

wordNotes.term: οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ (oinō oligō) — a little wine
wordNotes.explanation: Oinos is the general word for the product of the grape, used of a range of beverages in antiquity. Oligos means a small amount. The adjective restricts the counsel to a modest, medicinal portion tied to Timothy’s stomach and frequent illnesses, in harmony with Scripture’s repeated warnings about wine’s dangers.

verses.bibleText: Some men's sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment; and some men they follow after.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the brief aside, Paul returns to the subject of verse 22 and supplies the reason for patience in appointment. “Some men’s sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment.” The word “open” means plainly evident, conspicuous. Such sins run ahead of a person like heralds, announcing his character before he arrives. When a candidate’s faults are obvious, the decision is easy; his record has already pronounced the verdict.

“And some men they follow after.” Other people’s sins trail behind them, hidden at first and coming to light only later. A man may seem gifted, sincere, and capable while carrying pride, dishonesty, or impurity that only time will expose. This is precisely why Timothy must not lay hands on anyone in haste. Waiting allows the hidden to surface before the church has bound itself to an unworthy leader.

The immediate judgment in view is the church’s evaluation of candidates, but the language reaches beyond it. Every human life stands before the judgment of God, from whom nothing is concealed (Hebrews 4:13). “Be sure your sin will find you out” (Numbers 32:23). “God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing” (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Paul tells the Corinthians to judge nothing before the time, “until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

The image also carries a gospel truth. Sins that are confessed and forsaken may be said to go beforehand to judgment, for they are brought now to the One who “is faithful and just to forgive” (1 John 1:9) and covered by the intercession of Christ, our High Priest who “ever liveth to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25). Sins that are hidden and unrepented follow the sinner to the final reckoning, when the books are opened (Revelation 20:12). The wise course is to bring every hidden sin to Christ while mercy is offered.

For leaders who must choose others, the verse counsels deep humility and prayer. They cannot read hearts, first impressions deceive, and only patient observation and prayer guard the church from serious mistakes.

wordNotes.explanation: Prodēlos means clearly evident or manifest to all. The prefix intensifies more than it marks time. The only other New Testament use is Hebrews 7:14, “it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda.” Some sins are so obvious that no investigation is needed.

Epakoloutheō means to follow closely or come after. The same verb appears in verse 10 of the widow who “diligently followed every good work.” Here it pictures sins that trail behind a person and catch up with him later, becoming known only in time.

verses.bibleText: Likewise also the good works of some are manifest beforehand; and they that are otherwise cannot be hid.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final verse balances the warning with encouragement. “Likewise also the good works of some are manifest beforehand.” Just as some sins are obvious at once, so some people’s goodness is plain for all to see.

“And they that are otherwise cannot be hid.” The phrase “they that are otherwise” most naturally refers to good works that are not immediately evident, deeds done quietly, unnoticed by the crowd. Even these cannot stay hidden forever. The symmetry with verse 24 is complete: sins and good works alike may be evident now or revealed later, but nothing remains concealed indefinitely.

For Timothy the lesson is practical. Patience in appointment protects the church from unworthy leaders and helps it discover worthy ones who might otherwise be overlooked. The most conspicuous candidate is not always the best, and the humble servant working out of sight may be the one God has prepared.

For every believer the verse is a comfort. Jesus taught that the Father who sees in secret will reward openly (Matthew 6:4), and that the righteous will be surprised at the King’s remembrance of service they hardly noticed themselves (Matthew 25:37-40). “God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love” (Hebrews 6:10). Faithful service rendered without applause is never wasted.

wordNotes.term: τὰ ἄλλως ἔχοντα (ta allōs echonta) — they that are otherwise
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the things that are otherwise.” Allōs, found only here in the New Testament, means “in another way.” In parallel with verse 24 it most likely describes good works that are not yet evident, which nevertheless cannot remain concealed. Jesus said that nothing is hidden that shall not be made known.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What would change in a congregation if every act of correction, relief, and leadership were carried out as though among parents, brothers, and sisters?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Because the church is God’s household, its members honour one another with respect, practical provision, fair judgment, and tested integrity, and each family first cares for its own.
discussionQuestions: How does treating members as family shape the way correction is given and received?
Why does Paul place the first responsibility for widows on their own children and grandchildren?
What safeguards does Paul set around accusations against leaders, and why are both protection and public rebuke necessary?
What dangers follow when a church appoints leaders quickly on the strength of first impressions?
How does Paul’s counsel about Timothy’s health show concern for the whole person in ministry?
commonMisunderstandings: Paul does not teach that older members are beyond correction; he regulates the manner of correction.
The roll of widows does not mean that younger widows in need received no help; they were simply not placed on the permanent list.
Counsel for younger widows to remarry is advice for a specific situation, not a ruling on the worth or calling of every woman.
The little wine prescribed for Timothy’s illness is a limited, remedial measure, not permission for social drinking.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together compassion and discernment: the church gives generously and honours faithful service, yet it also refuses to subsidize neglect, idleness, or unproven leadership.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Ask God to make your home and your congregation places where the old are honoured, the lonely are supported, leaders are both cared for and held accountable, and every judgment is made as in his sight.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The God who defends the widow and sees every hidden deed calls people into a family where faith is shown in faithful love and where nothing is finally concealed from his judgment.
flow: God reveals himself as the protector of the widow, the orphan, and the lonely.
He forms a church that lives as a family and carries his care to the needy.
Faith that refuses to love one’s own household contradicts the gospel it professes.
Every person’s sins and good works will be brought to light before God.
Christ invites sinners to bring their sins to him now and to find a place in his family.
simpleIllustrations: A family table where grandparents are served first shows love more plainly than words spoken about honour.
A building inspector who signs off too quickly shares the blame when a hidden flaw brings down the roof; careful appointment protects everyone.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust the God who sees every hidden need and every hidden sin, and let him bring you into his family?
cautions: Do not present the church’s care as a reward earned by good works; it flows from God’s mercy to the needy.
Do not use verses 24-25 to frighten people without also presenting Christ’s forgiveness for confessed sin.
Do not suggest that widows or the poor are a burden; Paul’s concern is that every need be met by those best placed to meet it.

reflectionQuestions: When I must correct someone, do I speak to them as I would to my own father, mother, brother, or sister?
Which aging relative or lonely believer has a claim on my practical care that I have been leaving to others?
Do I honour faithful ministers with both respect and generous support, and do I refuse to entertain unproven charges against them?
Where am I tempted to show favouritism or to judge before I have heard the facts?
Am I content to let God bring my hidden service to light in his time, and am I bringing my hidden sins to him now?
